The tenth of the first lunar month; the Beginning of Spring.

Central Park lay south of the municipal government. Through the Yuan and the Ming both it had been the yamen of high provincial officials; at the start of the Qing, in the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, it was the mansion of the Prince Who Pacifies the South; and after the revolt was put down it became the office of the Governor of Guangdong. It was Mr. Sun who had proposed making it a park — a park that sold no tickets, where the townsfolk might come and go as they pleased.

Chen Qianli came into the park by the north gate and walked south along its central axis. In his short workman’s jacket he looked no different from the odd-job men at any of the government offices nearby. He seemed to be there simply to kill time, taking an interest in every sign that had writing on it, standing a moment before the Italian statue that Kang Youwei had presented, then staring a good while at the stone lions of the Prince of the South’s old mansion.

In truth he was sick with worry, his mind never still for a moment, wondering what he had done wrong. Perhaps he ought not to have let Ling Wen and Yi Junnian come to Guangdong; he had trusted his instinct too far, had not thought it through. Earlier he had taken Liang Shichao quietly to Shantou, and the business there had gone smoothly. Then they had turned by way of Hong Kong, meaning to take ship back to Shanghai, when they heard that something had happened at the Guangzhou liaison station — and that people sent by the Shanghai underground Party were caught up in it.

In the small hours they reached Guangzhou by steam-launch. First thing in the morning Chen Qianli had the Guangdong underground comrade who met him send word to Mo Shaoqiu; once they had made contact, Mo Shaoqiu took him at once to see Old Xiao. On the way, Mo Shaoqiu told Chen Qianli: “That morning Old Xiao came to the liaison station and arranged to meet Ling Wen the next day. But Ling Wen never came; he waited half an hour, then had no choice but to leave — one cannot linger long at a liaison station, that is the rule. Old Xiao went to the Tiannan Teahouse, leaving word that if Ling Wen came she was to find him there. Just past noon, the plainclothesmen of the detective squad arrived. We keep several lookouts posted around the station; day or night, if anyone suspicious moves about Jianglan Street, the station soon hears of it. Our man came straight back to warn us — but before he could get into the apothecary, shots rang out in the street.”
“They made the arrest at the teahouse first? They didn’t strike at both places at once?” Chen Qianli was a little puzzled.

“We thought it strange too. The moment the shots sounded we heard them at the station. As soon as the man got in and told us, I sent my wife out of the apothecary first. A liaison station is always kept ready to meet a sudden turn like this; there was nothing at the station that needed clearing away. Out on the terrace, behind the eaves-gutter, was an oilpaper packet with a pistol in it; my wife brought me the gun and slipped out by the back door. I went out the shop front, ran into Jianglan Street, and stood under the overhead arcade to see what was really going on. But they never came to the apothecary — not until dusk. Around five or six in the evening the plainclothesmen broke open the shop door and entered the station.”
Two schoolgirls came toward them along the lane; Mo Shaoqiu waited for them to pass, then went on:

“Yi Junnian says he and Ling Wen came to the liaison station together. Just as the two of them turned out of Shiqifu, the commotion broke out in front of the teahouse. They saw agents chasing Old Xiao and decided to split up. Yi Junnian went after them himself, telling Ling Wen to hurry to the apothecary — if the station was safe, she was to come in and report; if the station had been hit too, she was to go back first, to the Xinya Hotel, and wait for him there. Yi Junnian told Ling Wen they had an important task and must on no account take risks. He found a bicycle and caught up with Old Xiao at Yang Lane. Old Xiao had been cut off by two agents, one before and one behind, their guns leveled at him. Yi Junnian rode straight at them and with two shots killed the agents — but Old Xiao had been hit as well. Yi Junnian got Old Xiao to a safe place, then went back to find Ling Wen.

“But Ling Wen had vanished. He went back to the Xinya Hotel and waited until dusk — the two of them held tickets for that very night’s boat, only a few hours from sailing. Then Yi Junnian hurried over to bring us the news.”

Mo Shaoqiu led Chen Qianli to the neighborhood of Chailan, and in a shed by the water they found Old Xiao. The shed was built out over the bank, old boat-planks laid down for a floor, and on the planks Old Xiao lay unconscious.
“He drifts in and out; the doctor says he is not yet out of danger.”

The shed had been made over from an old wooden boat, and was itself like a cabin; its door faced onto the Donghao Creek, where Tanka skiffs crowded the water beyond counting. Boat-planks lay within and without, and only a cloth curtain hung across the doorway. Liang Shichao squatted outside the curtain smoking; Chen Qianli and Mo Shaoqiu sat within it, on the floor.

“Of Comrade Ling Wen there is no word at all — she has disappeared. My wife wept the moment she heard. She was so taken with the woman, taken with her from their first meeting; had it not been for the discipline of revolutionary work, she would have had her share her bed of a night and talk till dawn. My wife will not for a moment believe she is dead; she even went to make inquiries at the Public Security Bureau. We have a man inside the bureau — not a comrade exactly, but there’s no trouble in his finding a few things out. Yet the bureau had no word of anything: the Special Detective Section had taken no woman Communist. A murder? None either. Chinese New Year, they said — who commits murder at the New Year? The Guangzhou police and garrison rarely make a case or an arrest at this season, which is why their bursting into the teahouse the day before yesterday to seize Old Xiao is a very strange thing indeed.”
“The two of them — what did they do once they reached Guangzhou?” Chen Qianli asked, thinking as he spoke.

“The two of them came to the liaison station. We had long since had word from above that people from the Shanghai underground were coming. They came to set the courier line in order; we knew the Central leadership had some great move afoot. Ling Wen gave the recognition sign — of the two of them she was the leader. We went over every detail, fixed anew the recognition sign, the telephone, the telegraph registration, how to meet the boat, where they would lodge. When that was done, Ling Wen asked after her husband. The name Long Dong meant nothing to me — I only came to Guangzhou after the station was set up — but my wife knew it—”
Old Xiao broke suddenly into delirium, mumbling under his breath. Mo Shaoqiu rose and went to him, lifted the towel from his brow, wetted it in the basin, wrung it out, folded it, and laid it back.
“My wife had seen Long Dong, and had read the newspaper reports of that affair. She says it happened inside a certain house—”
“Where is this house Mrs. Mo speaks of?” The words were out of Chen Qianli before he knew it.
“Moat-Bowstring Street — Haoxian Road now, though the people of Guangzhou like to call it by its old name, Moat-Bowstring Street.”
Mo Shaoqiu explained the two street-names that sounded the same but were written with different characters.
“But they never went there. Yi Junnian says they had meant to go and look at Moat-Bowstring Street the next day, after meeting Old Xiao.”
Why had Old Xiao arranged to meet Ling Wen at the liaison station the next day? Chen Qianli turned it over privately.
Past the music pavilion was the park’s main gate. Out through it and across Gongyuan Road ran a small lane, and at the end of the lane, directly opposite, stood the Public Security Bureau.

The Public Security Bureau stood on Weixin North Road, and on the east side of the street, facing its gate, was a row of little shops. In the afternoon the eating-houses had all put out their fires; only the front of one fried-noodle stall was doing a brisk trade. A matting frame had been rigged over the door, with a few square tables and benches set out, and on the tables stood coarse green-glazed “quail” teapots — the customers were all drinking tea. The tea cost only five cents; the leaves were the spent dregs bought up from the great teahouses and re-roasted, and the only refreshment was taro cake. Every man of them had rolled up his sleeves and was chewing the fat, and the talk was of a big restaurant just opened at Xinzhen, whose real proprietor behind the scenes was Chen Weizhou, elder brother of Chen Jitang.

“—a great gambling house, fantan there, and if you back the right side you can win thousands of silver dollars. The moment the croupier’s rake stirs the beads, not a man at the table dares blink; you could hear a pin drop.”
“Little brother, you can talk — three thousand in chips just to get in the door; have you ever set foot in the place yourself?”

Liang Shichao too ordered a pot of tea, a plate of bean-sprout noodles, and two pieces of taro cake, and sat down at an empty table. Seeing a stranger at the next table, the others dropped their voices at once, and someone shot him a glance. Liang Shichao fished a pack of cigarettes from his jacket pocket and went round the neighboring table handing them out.

Pressed warmly to join them, and unable to refuse such goodwill, Liang Shichao moved to the next table. The tea-drinkers were all coolies and laborers from round about; not one of them could sit out a whole afternoon there, but only came in the breaks between jobs to snatch a seat and a mouthful of tea. People came and went; by the time Liang Shichao had drunk down half his pot, the table had turned over a fresh set of men.
He had picked up a thing or two, and when Chen Qianli came they moved to another empty table to talk.

“This noodle stall stays open late, and the police on the night shift often come by. Three years ago they found out one of the constables was a Communist — several of them still remember it. They say the Communist constable who was shot must have been known to Uncle Li at the cigarette shop next door; the man was forever coming in to buy his smokes.”

The two left the noodle stall, took a turn about the neighborhood, and came back to slip quietly into the cigarette shop. An old man sat inside. Liang Shichao hailed him as he stepped in: “Uncle Li.” The old man nodded.

The counter was a jumble of colors. Liang Shichao looked a long while, then picked out two packs of Three Castles, tucked one into his pocket, and handed the other to Chen Qianli. Paper packets lay on the counter; on the shelves behind stood tinned cigarettes. All at once Chen Qianli caught sight of two green tins set by themselves in a high corner, and something stirred in him.
He said to Uncle Li: “So you have Garrick here.”
Liang Shichao was about to put it into the local speech, but Uncle Li, as it turned out, had understood.
“Nobody buys them. If you want them, you can have them half price.”
“Done.” Chen Qianli drew out a silver dollar and handed it to the old man.
The tins were thick with dust. Chen Qianli found a rag on the counter and slowly wiped one clean.
“No one buys them; they’ve sat here more than three years.”
“If no one buys them, why stock them?”
“Back then someone did. The man who bought them died.”

Wiped clean of dust, the tin showed a sphinx. These were a superior cigarette, shipped over from England by great steamer, a whole silver dollar the tin. In a little shop like this, a customer who could afford the price might still not bring himself to spend it.
“I know who he was,” he said to Uncle Li. “A constable, and a Communist too.”

Uncle Li eyed him doubtfully; then, thinking that the two tins that had sat there three years were sold at last, he felt suddenly light of heart, and asked Chen Qianli: “You knew him? Are you a Communist too?”
Chen Qianli laughed aloud. “Me — a reporter for the Republican Daily. Where do you get these cigarettes in?”

“Officer Lu — no great rank, but for his smokes he’d have nothing else. In all these years, he was the only one who ever came to my shop for Garrick. He had me get the brand in; nowhere in all Guangzhou stocked it but the foreign houses on Shamian. Every month I’d bring in a few tins, and sell the lot to him.”
“And these two tins — why did he never come for them?”

“He came to buy on the afternoon of the Dragon Boat Festival, and I was out of stock. I told him to come for them the next day. The next day, he never came. Two days after that, the paper said he was dead.”
“The Dragon Boat Festival? Uncle Li, surely you misremember?”

“How could I misremember? It was Duanwu right enough — when he came I was just pasting the noon-hour charm on the shop door. The evening before, my daughter had gone home to her mother’s with rice-dumplings and pork, and the grown folk had taken the children down to the Pearl River to wash in the dragon-boat water. The house was busy, I couldn’t get away, so I could only go for the stock the next morning. Officer Lu came across from the other side, all smiles and spring breezes, with Little Phoenix on his arm. He said he’d come for them the next day.”

In the eighteenth year of the Republic the Dragon Boat Festival fell on the eleventh of June. On the thirteenth the Guangzhou Republican Daily carried the news that on the night of the ninth, Lu Zhongde, a Communist who had lain hidden within the Public Security Bureau, had been shot dead. Yet on the eleventh, the day of the festival, this Uncle Li had seen Lu Zhongde standing alive before him, come out of the Public Security Bureau, and looking as though some piece of good fortune had befallen him.

If the man announced as killed had not died, then some other man must have died, and gone unannounced. That man, Chen Qianli guessed, was very likely Long Dong, who was said to have escaped from the scene of the police arrest and never to have surfaced again — though of this he might never obtain certain proof. Not unless Ye Tao came back to life and drew from the innermost safe of Ye Qinian the record of the whole conspiracy.

Look at it from the other side: if the enemy declared Lu Zhongde a Communist and shot him dead, and yet afterward someone saw Lu Zhongde still alive, going about the places he always frequented — then why should the enemy have lied? That was a thing worth pondering.

Before he died, Old Fang had told Chen Qianli that in the seventh month of the eighteenth year of the Republic, to strengthen the intelligence work of the Shanghai underground, the organization had transferred Yi Junnian from Guangzhou to Shanghai — within the very month after Lu Zhongde had been declared dead in Guangzhou. Yi Junnian was a cover name used for secret work; in Guangzhou he had not gone by it, as he himself had told the comrades held with him in the Longhua lockup.

Before transferring Yi Junnian to Shanghai, his superiors had given him the contact methods, the signs, and this cover name, and sent him to make contact in Shanghai with Old Fang, the head of the underground. As for what name he had used in Guangzhou, he told no one — of course he could not, it was a matter of work discipline. To let slip a former name might endanger comrades still working in the old system.

But he liked to smoke, and smoked only the one brand — Garrick. In Guangzhou, too, there had been a man who liked that cigarette. A man, Chen Qianli thought, may for some purpose turn himself into another man. There are those who, like chameleons, can change identity, allegiance, shape, tone of voice, even character at will, shifting back and forth among roles as one puts on or takes off a coat. And yet, even so, such men will commonly keep one or two deep-rooted habits — out of arrogance, perhaps, or perhaps because, in his heart of hearts, a man always wants to hold on to some small thing that proves him to be himself.

He could not, of course, judge on instinct alone, nor on a tin of cigarettes alone. If only he had a photograph of Yi Junnian; then he could have had Uncle Li say whether the man was that Officer Lu of years ago.
Chen Qianli opened the green tin, tapped its bottom, drew out cigarettes for Uncle Li and Liang Shichao, and lit one himself.
“Officer Lu had Little Phoenix at his side?”

“The head-dresser lead of the Qunfangyan troupe, a female huadan. What a bewitching creature she was—” Uncle Li laid his Garrick away in a wooden box behind the counter. “I always said it, Officer Lu meeting her: it was the huadan meeting her young xiaosheng — husband, oh!”

Liang Shichao told Chen Qianli that in the Cantonese stage speech the words for “husband” and “suffering” sound the same. Uncle Li nodded and went on: “And sure enough he could not escape his death. In those days the two of them were all billing and cooing — little did they dream how it would end.”
“And this Little Phoenix — is she still singing?”
“At the Lehua. Lead huadan, the pillar of the troupe.”
